opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's really the big question for us right now. When we started with weight space learning, we built these model zoos ourselves, and that was very deliberate. We wanted controlled populations of neural networks: the same architecture, trained on the same data, with systematic variation in things like initialization, hyperparameters, and the number of training epochs. That gave us a clean, almost laboratory-like setting where we could ask whether you can learn meaningful representations directly from the weights. Can you predict a model's accuracy, its generalization gap, or which hyperparameters it was trained with, just by looking at its parameters? And the answer was yes, surprisingly well.

But of course the real world doesn't look like that. On Hugging Face you have hundreds of thousands of models, and they're extremely heterogeneous. Different architectures, different sizes, from small CNNs all the way up to billion-parameter transformers, trained on different data and different tasks, often with very sparse or inconsistent metadata. So you can't just take the methods that worked on a homogeneous zoo and scale them up directly.

There are a few challenges we think about. The first is heterogeneity of architecture. You need representations that can handle different layer types and shapes, so we've been working on tokenizing weights, breaking them into chunks that a transformer-style model can process regardless of where they came from. The second is symmetries. Neural networks have permutation symmetries, so many different weight configurations implement the same function, and your representation should respect that, either through augmentation or through equivariant architectures. The third is scale. Large models simply have too many parameters to ingest naively, so you need ways to subsample, compress, or work at the level of layers or components.

What makes Hugging Face so exciting, though, is that it's essentially a huge, naturally grown model zoo. A lot of those models are fine-tuned from the same base models, so there's actually a lot of structure there, like a family tree of models. If you can learn from that, you can start doing really interesting things: model retrieval, where you search for a model by its weights rather than its model card; predicting model quality before you even run it; detecting things like backdoors or problematic training data; or eventually generating new weights for a task directly.

So I see the move from controlled zoos to Hugging Face as going from the lab into the wild. The controlled zoos gave us the proof of concept and the understanding, and now the open model ecosystem gives us the data at scale. Our hope is that this turns neural network weights into a data modality in their own right, just like images or text.

r001.rationale: The response describes generating new weights as a potential use, but does not question the practical gain of doing so when a large model zoo must first be trained.

r002.rationale: It says heterogeneous architectures require weight representations that handle different layer types and shapes, and describes tokenizing weights into chunks processable regardless of their source.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's really the question we've been wrestling with, because the model zoos we trained ourselves were very clean. We'd take one architecture, say a small CNN, and train thousands of instances on MNIST or CIFAR with different seeds and hyperparameters. So everything was homogeneous. Same architecture, same layer ordering, same parameter count. That made it easy to treat a model as a point in weight space and learn representations over that population.

Hugging Face breaks every one of those assumptions. You have different architectures, different sizes, different tokenizers, models that are fine-tuned from the same base and models that have nothing to do with each other. And the metadata is often missing or wrong. So the first thing you lose is the notion of a fixed input dimensionality. You can't just flatten the weights and feed them to an encoder anymore.

The way we think about it is in a few steps. First, you have to move from a model-level representation to a layer-level or even a token-level representation. Treat a layer, or a chunk of a weight matrix, as the unit, and build the encoder so it's agnostic to how many of those units a model has, somewhat like how a transformer handles variable-length sequences. Second, you have to deal with the symmetries in weight space. Permutations of neurons, scaling between layers, these give you functionally identical models that look completely different as raw vectors. In a homogeneous zoo you could partially ignore that or augment your way around it, but in the wild you really have to build it into the representation.

And then third, which I find the most interesting, is what the signal actually is. The thing that makes Hugging Face compelling is lineage. Most models there are fine-tunes of a few base models. So the structure we care about isn't necessarily "what accuracy does this model have," it's "where did it come from, what was it fine-tuned on, how far did it move from its parent." That's a very natural thing to learn in weight space, because fine-tuning typically moves you in a low-dimensional subspace relative to the base. You can start to see families of models, and you can start to ask questions like, is this model a derivative of a licensed base, or has this model been trained on data it shouldn't have seen.

So the honest answer is that we're not fully there. The pretrained zoos we built were almost a laboratory setting. Hugging Face is the real world, and it forces us to make the methods architecture-agnostic, symmetry-aware, and much more focused on relationships between models rather than isolated properties of a single one. But that's also where it becomes useful beyond a research curiosity, because that's where the models people actually use live.

r001.rationale: The response notes that the researchers trained thousands of models in a homogeneous zoo, but it does not question the practical gain of generating a new network given that prerequisite.

r002.rationale: It says heterogeneous architectures cannot be handled by flattening weights and proposes layer- or chunk-level units with an encoder agnostic to the number of units, communicating the need for architecture-flexible weight tokenization.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting question is whether we can move from a model zoo that we construct under controlled conditions to a population of models that people have trained independently. In a controlled zoo, you can keep the architecture fixed and vary the initialization, the hyperparameters, or the training data. That gives you a way to study what information is actually present in the weights.

With models on Hugging Face, you have much more diversity, but also much less control. Models can have different architectures, different training histories, and different tasks. And many of them are fine-tuned versions of the same base model, so they’re not independent samples. If you ignore that relationship, you might think you’ve learned something general when you’re really just recognizing a model family.

So I would approach it incrementally. Start with models that share an architecture, or even a common pretrained checkpoint, and ask what we can learn from the differences in their weights. Can we predict their performance? Can we identify which model is useful for a new task without evaluating every candidate? Then broaden the representation to accommodate more variation.

That’s the transition: from demonstrating that learning in weight space works in a controlled setting to understanding which properties transfer across a much more heterogeneous collection of models.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses the limits of a controlled model zoo and possible uses for weight-space learning, but does not question the practical gain of generating a new network after first training a large zoo.

r002.rationale: The candidate notes that Hugging Face models vary in architecture and says to broaden the representation, but does not identify adapting a weight tokenizer to arbitrary architectures as necessary.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a very exciting next step, because a model zoo gives us a controlled setting. We can train models with the same architecture, vary the initialization or the hyperparameters, and study what information is actually encoded in their weights. But then the question is: how much of what we learn in that setting transfers to a much broader population of models?

With Hugging Face, you have models trained by different people, on different datasets, for different tasks. And the first challenge is that these models don’t necessarily live in the same weight space. They have different architectures and different sizes, and even within the same architecture, you have symmetries—two models can implement a similar function without their parameters being directly aligned.

So I would start with families of compatible models, perhaps models fine-tuned from the same pretrained checkpoint. That gives you a shared starting point, and you can ask whether a representation of their weights tells you something useful about their behavior: which model might work for your task, how it might transfer, or which models might be good candidates to combine.

The opportunity is to make this collection something we can learn from collectively. But moving from a controlled model zoo to that setting is also the test of whether our representations capture something general, rather than just the particular way we constructed the zoo.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether findings from a controlled model zoo generalize, but does not question the practical gain of generating a new network when a large zoo must first be trained.

r002.rationale: It notes that heterogeneous models have different architectures and suggests starting with compatible families, but does not identify adapting the weight tokenizer to arbitrary architectures as necessary.
